title: Progress Is a Squiggly Line, Not a Straight One
excerptForBlog:
AWS followed lots of squiggly lines, too. The original vision included storage, compute, payments, and human intelligence. Some of those (e.g. storage and compute) became lynchpins in AWS. Others didn't succeed. We didn't initially plan a database service; and when we built one, our first attempt failed to get traction. We went back to the drawing board and built new relational and non-relational database services, which have resonated well and become core to millions of AWS applications.

There's a band I like from New Zealand called 'The Beths,' who've written several excellent records, with thought-provoking lyrics. When their latest album dropped last summer titled 'Straight Line Was a Lie,' it made me think about how prescient that expression is. Most long-term endeavors do not follow a linear straight line, up and to the right. Progress jumps around; it'll zig up, then sometimes stall, or zag down, or force you back to the starting line. That's because the world is complex, and new technology, business model invention, competitors, global issues, or people and cultural shifts can come into play.

We're in the middle of some of the biggest inflections of our lifetime (e.g. AI, robotics, space industrialization, geopolitical and military conflict). And, just as proficient golfers need to be skilled across driving, approach shots, chipping, and putting, durable companies must be adept at managing different elements of inflections.

Wherever possible, invent the next inflections. We try to anticipate what will make customers' lives easier and better every day, and invent the next inflection. Historically, we've successfully done so in areas like Retail, Logistics, AWS, Ads, Kindle, Alexa, and Pharmacy.

lessonTitle: Progress Is a Squiggly Line, Not a Straight One
lessonBody:
## 1. Core Message
Jassy uses AWS's own history to make a simple point: big bets rarely go in a straight line. AWS's original plan included things that worked (storage, compute) and things that didn't (human intelligence, the first database attempt). The lesson he draws is that durable companies must be able to handle setbacks, restarts, and major inflections — and, where possible, create the next inflection themselves.

## 2. What the Executive Is Really Thinking
Jassy is setting expectations with shareholders. Amazon is spending heavily across AI, robotics, and space — areas where results will be uneven. By naming past failures inside AWS (a service "core to millions of AWS applications" today started with a failed first attempt), he is buying patience for current bets. He is also framing Amazon as a company that doesn't just react to inflections — it tries to "invent the next inflection," citing Retail, Logistics, AWS, Ads, Kindle, Alexa, and Pharmacy as proof.

## 3. Key Management Lessons

### Plan for the squiggle, not the straight line
#### What it means
Long projects move in jumps. They "zig up, then sometimes stall, or zag down, or force you back to the starting line."
#### Why it matters
Leaders who promise straight-line progress lose credibility the moment reality bends. Leaders who pre-warn about the squiggle keep trust through the dips.
#### MBA Perspective
This is closest to Resource-Based View thinking: the lasting advantage is not any single product, but the organizational capacity to absorb setbacks and keep building.
#### Real-world application
When pitching a multi-year initiative to a board, show the expected non-linear path — the likely stalls and resets — instead of a tidy hockey stick. It changes how setbacks get interpreted later.

### Kill the first version when it doesn't get traction
#### What it means
Amazon's "first attempt failed to get traction," so they "went back to the drawing board and built new relational and non-relational database services."
#### Why it matters
Most teams defend a weak v1 because shipping it cost so much. The faster move is to admit it didn't resonate and rebuild around what customers actually need.
#### MBA Perspective
Disruptive Innovation logic: the early version exists to learn what the market really wants. The second build, informed by real usage, is usually where the moat forms.
#### Real-world application
Set an explicit "traction test" before launch — usage thresholds at 6 and 12 months. If the product misses, the default action is rebuild, not patch.

### Be a multi-skilled company, not a one-trick one
#### What it means
Jassy's golf analogy: "proficient golfers need to be skilled across driving, approach shots, chipping, and putting." Durable companies must be "adept at managing different elements of inflections."
#### Why it matters
In a moment with several simultaneous shifts ("AI, robotics, space industrialization, geopolitical and military conflict"), one-dimensional companies get caught flat-footed on the dimensions they ignored.
#### MBA Perspective
Platform Strategy: companies built as platforms can ride multiple inflections at once because each new capability plugs into the existing base.
#### Real-world application
Audit your leadership team: do you have depth in each of the major shifts hitting your industry, or only the one you're most comfortable with? Hire or train against the gap.

### Try to invent the next inflection yourself
#### What it means
"Wherever possible, invent the next inflections." Don't only react to change — try to be the cause of it.
#### Why it matters
Reacting to an inflection puts you behind incumbents who saw it earlier. Creating one resets the competitive board on your terms.
#### MBA Perspective
First-Mover Advantage, when paired with the scale to defend the position. Amazon's listed wins (Retail, Logistics, AWS, Ads, Kindle, Alexa, Pharmacy) show a pattern of entering categories before they were obvious.
#### Real-world application
Reserve a small portion of budget and headcount for bets that have no current customer demand but anticipate "what will make customers' lives easier and better every day."

## 4. Strategic Analysis (MBA Style)

### Competitive Strategy
The strategy is portfolio-based: place many bets, accept that some will fail, double down on the ones that resonate. AWS itself is the proof point — some original pillars stuck, others didn't, and the company kept building.

### Risk Analysis
The risk Jassy is naming is the risk of being caught flat on a major inflection. He lists four happening at once. The implied danger: a company optimized for only one of them — say, AI — could be blindsided by the others.

### Build vs Buy Analysis
The document only shows the build side. AWS's database services were built, failed, and rebuilt internally. The implicit logic: when a capability is core to the platform, building gives you the freedom to scrap and restart without unwinding an acquisition.

### Market Dynamics
Jassy describes a market shaped by simultaneous, overlapping inflections. That favors companies with broad platforms and deep balance sheets over focused specialists, because the cost of covering all the bases is high.

### Long-Term Strategic Implications
If Amazon succeeds at "inventing the next inflection," it compounds its position across more categories — the Kindle/Alexa/Pharmacy pattern repeats. If it fails, the heavy spending across AI, robotics, and space becomes a drag with no payoff, and shareholders will judge the squiggle story less generously.

## 5. Hidden Insights
- **Pre-buying patience.** By opening the letter with failures inside AWS, Jassy is conditioning shareholders to accept the misses that will surface inside today's AI and robotics spending.
- **AWS as the canonical case.** Every founder-CEO has a founding myth; Jassy, who didn't found Amazon, is anchoring his credibility to AWS — the business he is most associated with building.
- **Quiet signal on capital allocation.** Listing four inflections (AI, robotics, space, geopolitics) tells investors where the capex is going without giving numbers.
- **The list of past wins is a defense.** Naming Retail, Logistics, AWS, Ads, Kindle, Alexa, and Pharmacy — a mix of huge hits and smaller ones — quietly argues that even Amazon's less-celebrated bets count as inflection-creation.
pullQuote: Durable companies don't bet on one straight line — they build the muscle to zig, zag, and start over without losing momentum.
